comparisons.summary: Same family, same 9 mm poles, one size apart. The Rock 22 is the sturdier-reviewed two-person tent; the Rock 32 adds about 9 square feet and big vestibules, and owners are more split on its waterproofing.
comparisons.pickA: You're one or two people, want a tent owners trust in hard rain and wind, and mostly car camp or take short hikes.
comparisons.pickB: You're two people who want real elbow room or three on summer trips, and you'll put a footprint under the thinner floor.

comparisons.summary: The two classic North Face two-person tents. The Tadpole 23 is over a pound lighter and has a vestibule big enough to cook in, but it's tight for two with one door. The Rock 22 is heavier and roomier, with two doors.
comparisons.pickA: You backpack, often solo or with one close partner, and pack weight matters more than space.
comparisons.pickB: You're two people who each want a door, and you mostly camp near the car or hike in short distances.

comparisons.summary: The newer Tadpole 2 swapped the Tadpole 23's three crossing poles for a hubbed DAC frame and dropped weight, but the vestibule shrank to about 9 square feet. Poles don't interchange between the two.
comparisons.pickA: You want the lighter, stiffer hubbed frame and you're mostly solo or two compact people in summer.
comparisons.pickB: You want the bigger cooking vestibule and the classic three-pole pitch, and the fly coating on your tent is still sound.

comparisons.summary: The 2-Meter Dome replaced the Dome 8. The newer tent has more floor (about 167 vs 128 square feet) and a twelve-pole Easton frame; the Dome 8 uses a DAC hub-and-pole set and packs lighter at about 35 lb versus roughly 50.
comparisons.pickA: You want a proven storm-worthy group basecamp at a lower weight and you're patient with a slow first pitch.
comparisons.pickB: You need the most stand-up living space for a stationary expedition camp and can haul about 50 lb.
keywords: north face 2 meter dome vs dome 8

comparisons.summary: Both are hubbed four-season DAC domes with three big doors. The Dome 5 is the smaller team tent at about 18 lb trail weight; the Dome 8 is a full stand-up basecamp with a 34-square-foot vestibule and a 35 lb pack.
comparisons.pickA: You're a small team hauling by sled or vehicle and want a four-season dome that's easier to move.
comparisons.pickB: You need stand-up headroom for a group at a long stationary camp in severe weather.

comparisons.summary: A four-season expedition tent against a three-season tent of similar size. The Mountain 25 is the one owners call bombproof in gales and heavy snow, at about 3.5 lb more trail weight. The Rock 22 is the comfortable, cheaper choice for everything but winter.
comparisons.pickA: You camp in winter, above treeline or in the worst weather you expect to see, and accept the weight and slower pitch.
comparisons.pickB: You camp spring through fall and want a roomy two-door tent that's cooler on summer nights.
keywords: north face 4 season vs 3 season tent

comparisons.summary: Two light two-person backpacking tents. The Meso 22 is lighter and roomier on paper, with owners reporting it steady in 50+ mph gusts; the Tadpole 23 is the long-time favorite with a cook-sized vestibule. Neither is generous for two tall people.
comparisons.pickA: You want the lighter pack and you'll bring extra stakes for the fly.
comparisons.pickB: You want a proven freestanding pitch and a vestibule you can cook in, mostly as a solo tent.

comparisons.summary: Close twins on paper: both about 43.5 square feet with the same published weights. The difference is in the details. The Rock 32 uses 9 mm poles; the Roadrunner 33 mixes 9.6 mm and 9 mm DAC poles with an all-mesh canopy, and its corners can stick out past the fly.
comparisons.pickA: You want the easier-to-find tent with one pole size, for summer trips and car camping.
comparisons.pickB: You want maximum airflow in heat and two people each with a door and a large vestibule.

comparisons.summary: Two freestanding three-person tents. The Manta Ray 33 has a bigger T-shaped floor (51 vs 43.5 square feet), big vestibules and a gear loft, and owners say it's silent in 40–50 mph wind. The Rock 32 is a little lighter and a simpler pitch.
comparisons.pickA: You want the most room and the steadiest tent in wind, and you'll add stakes and keep the doors closed in rain.
comparisons.pickB: You want a slightly lighter, quick-pitching tent for summer trips with two or three people.
keywords: north face manta ray vs rock 32

comparisons.summary: Two light, fast-pitching two-person tents with condensation as the shared weak spot. The Vario 23 is single-wall with an exoskeleton frame and more floor; the Spectrum 23 is a little lighter and smaller, and owners say it's strong in wind.
comparisons.pickA: You're two people who want to sit up and pitch fast, mostly in dry weather.
comparisons.pickB: You're solo in dry or breezy places and want the lightest, most compact option.

comparisons.summary: Two solo tents from different eras. The Mica 12 is the lighter, freestanding one that fits a 6-foot-3 camper. The Arcus pitches fast with clip-and-hook pole joints and a pre-bent vestibule pole, but it's much heavier for one person.
comparisons.pickA: You're backpacking solo and want the lighter pack.
comparisons.pickB: You're a tall solo camper, often near the car, and want a quick pitch and a light summer fly.

comparisons.summary: Both are freestanding two-door, two-vestibule tents for two at around 5 lb. The Minibus 23 uses reverse-combi poles for steeper walls and has a 20-square-foot vestibule area; the Rock 22 has far more owner reports behind it, including staying put in 70 mph gusts.
comparisons.pickA: You want two vestibules with more storage and the steeper-wall pole design, and the coatings on your tent are sound.
comparisons.pickB: You want the tent with the longer track record in rain and wind.

comparisons.b: The North Face Double Headed Toad 44 BX
comparisons.summary: Two four-person tents built for different trips. The Wawona 4 is a 13 lb car-camping tent you can stand up in, with a huge porch vestibule. The Double Headed Toad 44 BX is about 7.5 lb, light enough for short backpacking trips with a family, and owners say it holds up in hard rain and wind.
comparisons.pickA: You car camp and want standing room and a covered porch for chairs.
comparisons.pickB: You hike in with a small family and need a four-person tent you can carry.
